one_liner: Single-file C dynamic R-tree with O(1) copy-on-write clones; inserts 20-40x faster than Boost.Geometry's R*-tree.
what_it_does: rtree.c is a dynamic, in-memory R-tree over axis-aligned rectangles; a point is inserted as a rectangle whose max corner equals its min. You pass coordinate arrays plus a void* payload to rtree_insert/rtree_delete, and rtree_search calls your callback for every item intersecting a query window. rtree_scan, rtree_count, rtree_rect and an O(1) copy-on-write rtree_clone complete the API. Dimensions (default 2), coordinate type (double), payload type (void*) and node fan-out (64) are compile-time macros, settable as RTREE_DIMS, RTREE_NUMTYPE, RTREE_DATATYPE and RTREE_MAXITEMS since v0.6.1. It is a plain C API, not a replacement for boost::geometry::index::rtree.
how_it_is_fast: Insertion is a cheap Guttman R-tree variant rather than R*: descending, it takes the first child whose rectangle already contains the new item, otherwise the child with least area enlargement. It never computes overlap and never does R*'s forced reinsertion, which is where Boost's insert cost goes. A full node is split in one linear pass ('edge snap'): each entry goes to whichever edge of the node's largest axis it is nearer, with no sorting since v0.6.0. Nodes are wide (64 entries) and keep their 64 rectangles in one contiguous array beside the child or payload array, so a search scans packed coordinates with branch-light intersect tests. Deletion only unlinks emptied nodes and never condenses or reinserts, which keeps erase cheap.
when_to_use: Dynamic 2D sets with heavy churn (moving entities, live map features, geofences, editors): in GeoToolbox's insert/erase/reinsert/query scenario, insert was 21-41x, erase 2.8-4.1x and reinsert 8-10x faster than Boost R*-tree (geomeans), and the whole scenario 4.8-6.4x faster (11-13x at 10^6 elements). All ratios derived from page data

Point or box keys with window (intersects) queries on 10^3-10^6 elements when the index is built and updated by insertion. Range queries afterwards were at parity with a dynamically built Boost tree (1.00-1.12x geomean) and up to about 2x faster at 10^4-10^5 elements (derived from page data)
C code or FFI that wants one MIT-licensed .c/.h pair with no dependencies and a custom malloc/free hook
Snapshot isolation: rtree_clone is O(1) and copies nodes lazily on write, so readers can keep an old version while a writer mutates a clone
Input you can pre-sort along a Hilbert curve: the README's 1M-point run drops insert from 151 to 73 ns/op and item search from 242 to 83 ns/op compared with random order
when_not_to_use: Nearest-neighbour or kNN queries: there are none. Use nanoflann (points), GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or Boost R*-tree

Static, query-heavy data: there is no bulk load (STR or Hilbert packing). After an insert-built load, range queries were 0.80-0.92x the speed of Boost's packed tree (geomean), and KdBoxTree is faster still. Insert-built loading itself was 1.3-1.5x faster than Boost's packing (derived from page data)
Tiny sets of about 10^2 elements: range queries ran at 0.3-0.7x Boost's speed and the full insert/erase/query scenario at 0.33-0.79x (derived from page data)
Tight memory: at 10^6 2D keys it used about 58-70 MB against Boost 43 MB, KdBoxTree 30-50 MB and nanoflann 8-17 MB (GeoToolbox memory deltas)
Several dimensions or coordinate types in one program: one DIMS/NUMTYPE per compiled copy of rtree.c. GeoToolbox measured only 2D with double coordinates

integration.dependencies: none (libc; <stdatomic.h> for copy-on-write reference counts unless RTREE_NOATOMICS is defined)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (stdatomic.h, compound literals in the examples); MSVC needs RTREE_NOATOMICS or /experimental:c11atomics, which GeoToolbox handles that way. From C++, compile rtree.c as C
integration.platforms: any; portable C with no SIMD or platform code
integration.thread_safety: not documented. From the code: rtree_search and rtree_scan take a const tree and write nothing, so concurrent readers without a writer look safe, and clones share nodes through atomic reference counts, so separate clones can be mutated on separate threads unless RTREE_NOATOMICS is set

gotchas: rtree.h has no extern "C" guard, so wrap the include from C++. Its prototypes hard-code double coordinates and a void* payload, and since v0.6.0 rtree.c no longer includes rtree.h. Changing RTREE_NUMTYPE/RTREE_DATATYPE without editing the header therefore compiles silently against mismatched types (inferred from code; the README says to edit the header to match)

rtree_delete needs a bit-identical rectangle and the same payload pointer (memcmp, or a comparator via rtree_delete_with_comparator), and removes only the first match. It returns true even when nothing matched, so check rtree_count if you need to know

The published numbers are for older code. GeoToolbox pinned v0.5.3 (May 2024), and the README's run dates from 2023. v0.6.0 (2026-09-05) removed the 10% minimum fill on splits (a node may hold one entry), removed sort-on-split and turned path hints off by default, and no benchmark of the current code is published

The README's algorithm notes (ties go to the smallest area; an 'equal' bucket during splits) do not match the current code, which keeps the first least-enlargement child and sends ties to the left node. Deletes never refill underfull nodes, so heavy deletion can leave sparse nodes
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over GeoToolbox KdBoxTree and nanoflann when the set changes continuously, since neither supports erase. Pick it over THST when you want a plain C, MIT-licensed dynamic tree with copy-on-write snapshots. For static data, or when you need nearest-neighbour queries, KdBoxTree (boxes) or nanoflann (points) are faster, and TG covers polygon predicates rather than indexing.
verified_claims_summary: The independent GeoToolbox suite compared rtree.c v0.5.3 (compiled as C with RTREE_NOATOMICS, 2D, double) with Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree on 25 point and 44 box dataset/size combinations of 10^2-10^6 elements. It was built with MSVC 2026 and clang-cl 22 (Release, /arch:AVX2 and LTO per its public CMakeLists) on an ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop under Windows 11, CPU model not stated. The result TSVs show dynamic insert/erase/reinsert far faster than Boost: insert 21-41x, erase 2.8-4.1x, reinsert 8-10x and the scenario total 4.8-6.4x (geomeans). Range queries were at parity (1.00-1.12x) after dynamic builds and slightly slower (0.80-0.92x) than Boost's bulk-loaded tree (all ratios derived from page data). The author's own README reports 151 ns/op insert and 242 ns/op item search on 1M random points (clang-17 -O3, Ryzen 9 5950X) with no Boost comparison.
status_note: Maintained by a single author (v0.6.1 tagged 2026-09-06, last commit 2026-09-21, 149 stars, 2 open issues), MIT-licensed and about 800 lines of C, so easy to vendor. Pin a tag, because v0.6.0 changed the split rules after the published benchmarks.
